"Instead of" means "in place of" or "rather than."

It is used to show that one thing was chosen, done, or used while another thing was not. The thing that comes after "instead of" is always the thing that did not happen — the rejected, skipped, or replaced option.

Think of it this way: every "instead of" sentence has two sides —

  • What DID happen (the choice that was made)
  • What did NOT happen (the thing after "instead of")

She drank tea instead of coffee.

Here, she drank tea (this happened). She did not drink coffee (this is what "instead of" points to). Coffee was replaced by tea.
The Grammar Rule: What Follows "Instead of"

"Instead of" is a preposition, so it must be followed by a noun, a pronoun, or a gerund (verb + -ing). It cannot be followed by a bare verb.

Noun:

He ordered soup instead of a salad.

Pronoun:

They called you instead of me.

Gerund (verb + -ing):

She went for a walk instead of watching TV.

❌ Wrong: She went for a walk instead of watch TV.
✅ Right: She went for a walk instead of watching TV.

This is one of the most important grammar rules for this word. Whenever a verb follows "instead of," it must take the -ing form.

1. Substitution — One thing replaces another

This is the most basic use. Something takes the place of something else.

Use olive oil instead of butter.

(Olive oil replaces butter.)

The meeting was held online instead of in person.

(Online replaced in-person.)

Can you send an email instead of a letter?

(Email replaces the letter.)

Here, there is no strong judgment. One option simply swaps out for another.

2. Choice or Preference — Picking one option over another

When you make a deliberate choice between two options, "instead of" expresses what you picked and what you passed on.

I decided to study medicine instead of law.

(I chose medicine; I did not choose law.)

They bought a house instead of renting one.

(They chose buying; they did not rent.)

She stayed home instead of going to the party.

(She chose to stay home; she did not go.)

The two options are presented as alternatives, and one is selected over the other.

3. Correction — Replacing something wrong with something right

"Instead of" is used to say: stop doing this, do that.

Say "may I" instead of "can I."

(Use "may I"; stop using "can I.")

Try to listen instead of just talking.

(Listening is recommended; talking is discouraged.)

Write it in your own words instead of copying it.

(Original writing is expected; copying is rejected.)

In this use, "instead of" often carries a corrective or instructive tone.

4. Contrast with What Was Expected — Pointing out a surprising or disappointing choice

Sometimes "instead of" highlights that someone did something unexpected — often something they should not have done, when they should have done something else.

Instead of apologizing, he made excuses.

(We expected an apology; he gave excuses instead.)

Instead of helping, she just stood there.

(Helping was expected; standing there was the actual behaviour.)

He spent the money on games instead of paying the bills.

(Paying bills was the responsible thing to do; he chose games.)

Notice in these examples, the thing after "instead of" is often what was expected, needed, or more sensible. The sentence quietly criticizes or highlights the contrast.
A Subtle but Important Point: "Instead of" Points to the Absent Thing

This is worth understanding deeply. The phrase "instead of" always points at the thing that is missing from the situation — the thing that was not done, not used, not chosen.

He wore a jacket instead of a coat.

The coat is absent. The jacket is present.

She cried instead of speaking.

Speech is absent. Crying is present.

This is why the phrase is so useful — it lets you name both what happened and what did not happen in a single sentence. The main part of the sentence tells the reader what exists; "instead of" tells the reader what is absent.

It is worth knowing how it differs from "instead" used alone.

"Instead of" (preposition) must be followed by a noun, pronoun, or gerund:

She called me instead of you.

"Instead" (adverb) stands alone, usually at the end of a sentence or after a comma. It refers back to an option already mentioned:

She did not call you. She called me instead.

Both mean the same thing, but "instead of" names the rejected option right there in the sentence, while "instead" (alone) relies on context already established.

Mistake 1: Using a bare verb after "instead of"
❌ He ran instead of walk.
✅ He ran instead of walking.

Always use the -ing form after "instead of."

Mistake 2: Confusing which side is which

A learner sometimes writes "instead of" backwards. Remember: the thing after "instead of" is the one that did NOT happen.

He texted instead of calling.

Texting happened. Calling did not happen.

If you are unsure, ask yourself: which action actually took place? That one goes before "instead of." The one that was skipped or replaced goes after it.

Mistake 3: Using "instead of" when you mean "except for" or "apart from"

"Instead of" is about replacement or rejection. It does not mean the same as "except for."

❌ Everyone came instead of John. (This sounds odd — it implies someone replaced John, which is not the intended meaning.)
✅ Everyone came except for John.

Use "instead of" only when one thing genuinely substitutes for or replaces another.

"Instead of" is a preposition meaning "in place of" or "rather than." It introduces the thing that was not chosen, not done, or not used — the absent or replaced option. What actually happened is found in the main part of the sentence. It is always followed by a noun, pronoun, or verb in the -ing form, never a bare verb. Its uses range from simple substitution and personal choice to correction and contrast with what was expected. In every case, the core logic is the same: something took the place of something else, and "instead of" names the thing that lost its place.
